text: Russia's plan for a quick decapitation of Ukraine failed near Kyiv in 2022.
In summer 2022 Russian massed artillery ground forward in Donbas.
In autumn 2022 Ukraine exploited an overstretched Russian force in Kharkiv Oblast and levered Russia out of right-bank Kherson.
Russia answered the 2022 Ukrainian counteroffensives with mobilization, annexation claims and a long-range strike campaign using Iranian-designed Shaheds.
Wagner and convict "meat assaults" took Bakhmut in the 2023 attritional phase.
Ukraine's Western-equipped 2023 offensive stalled in about 30 km of prepared Russian defences.
While US aid was stalled, Russia used its shell and glide-bomb superiority to take Avdiivka.
From mid-2024 tactical UAVs became the main killer, and the drone "kill zone" made manoeuvre very costly.
Russia gained about 3,600 km² in 2024 and about 4,300–4,800 km² in 2025, depending on the tracker, buying slow gains at huge cost.
Ukraine raided Kursk and struck deep into Russia (Operation Spiderweb) in the drone-dominated phase.
notes: This sentence of the overview carries no inline citation of its own; the block cites the CSIS and DeepState sources for the adjacent point.

text: Ukraine scaled interceptor drones against about 50,000 Shaheds a year.
From late January 2026 Ukraine turned local counterattacks into real gains, helped by Russia's loss of Starlink.
By September 2026 ISW assessed that Russia had made "near-zero net gains since March 2026".
Aid to Ukraine shifted from US-led gifting (2022–2024), through the US drawdown and two brief 2025 pauses, to European-financed support and European purchases of US weapons via PURL (2025–2026).
notes: Spans all eras e1–e9.

text: From March 2026 the US–Iran war competed with Ukraine for the same Patriot and ATACMS stocks.
As of late September 2026 there was no durable ceasefire in the Russo-Ukrainian war.
As of late September 2026 Russia still demanded all of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson oblasts, neutrality and demilitarization, and Ukraine refused.
Before 2022 Russia occupied Crimea plus part of Donbas.
notes: Uncited bullet in the territory anchors block; attached to the block's DeepState source.

text: DeepState's end-2025 total of Russian-occupied territory was just over 116,000 km².
DeepState's net Russian gains were 4,336 km² in 2025, about 3,600 km² in 2024 and about 110–140 km² in 2023.
In 2023 Russia took 540 km² and Ukraine regained about 430 km² (DeepState).
At end-2025 Russia occupied just over 19% of Ukraine according to DeepState.
At end-2025 Russia occupied about 20% of Ukraine, or about 120,000 km², according to CSIS.
In 2026 Ukraine regained several hundred km² of territory.
DeepStateMAP is the live reference for frontline geometry.
Computed from DeepState's map versions, Russian gains in 2024 come to about 3,300 km², against the 3,600+ km² DeepState published.
Computed from DeepState's map versions, net Russian gains were about 380–390 km² a month in e7–e8, falling to about 78 km² a month in e9.
Computed from DeepState's map versions, the grey zone roughly tripled, to about 1,600–1,800 km².
notes: The source text does not give the baseline date of the tripling.

text: CSIS estimates Russian casualties to December 2025 at about 1.2 million, of whom 275,000–325,000 were killed.
British intelligence estimates about 1.5 million Russian casualties and about 500,000 killed.
The Ukrainian General Staff claims 1.52 million Russians "liquidated" (killed or seriously wounded).
Mediazona and BBC Russian had confirmed 258,980 Russian dead by name as of September 2026, a hard lower bound.
Russian losses per km² gained rose from 53 (ISW, Sep–Nov 2024) to 85 (2025) and about 290 (2026), per Radio Svoboda using General Staff and DeepState data.
CSIS estimates Ukrainian casualties to December 2025 at 500,000–600,000, of whom 100,000–140,000 were killed.
Oryx has visually confirmed 24,138 Russian equipment losses, including 4,448 tanks.
In February–March 2014 the Revolution of Dignity (Euromaidan) ended with Yanukovych fleeing Ukraine.
In February–March 2014 Russian troops without insignia occupied Crimea, and Russia annexed it after an illegitimate "referendum".
From April to September 2014 Russian-backed forces seized towns in Donbas and the "DPR/LPR" were proclaimed.
Malaysia Airlines flight MH17 was shot down over Donbas in July 2014.
At Ilovaisk in August–September 2014 regular Russian troops intervened directly and defeated Ukrainian forces.
In February 2015 the battle of Debaltseve was fought and the Minsk II agreements were signed.
After February 2015 the Donbas line froze into trench warfare, with ceasefire violations but little change in territory.
About 14,000 people were killed in the Donbas war in 2014–2021.
The first US Javelin sales, 210 missiles in 2018 and 150 more in 2019, gave Ukraine a modern anti-armour capability before the invasion.
In 2021 Russian forces massed on Ukraine's borders, setting up the February 2022 invasion.
By 2022 Ukraine had eight years of combat-experienced brigades (ATO/JFO veterans) and a partly NATO-trained officer corps.
notes: The text marks this sim-relevance point as background, not separately sourced; cited to the block source as background.

text: By 2022 Russia had an occupied Donbas base for its forces and had already set up the "DPR/LPR" militia corps.
notes: Background, not separately sourced in the text.

text: On 24 February 2022 a multi-axis Russian invasion from Belarus, Russia and Crimea hit Kyiv (Hostomel, Bucha, Irpin), Chernihiv, Sumy, Kharkiv and the south.
In the south, Russia took Kherson and besieged Mariupol in the invasion phase of 2022.
Russia planned a roughly 10-day operation and expected occupation of Ukraine by August 2022.
Russia's deception worked at the start of the invasion, but it had no contingency plan when speed failed.
By early April 2022 Russia had abandoned the attempt on Kyiv and the north.
The Mariupol siege ran on into May 2022.
notes: Uncited sentence; attached to the block source Wikipedia.

text: In the invasion phase Ukraine fought with pre-war stocks plus rapid Western light anti-armour and MANPADS deliveries (Javelin, NLAW, Stinger) and Bayraktar TB2s.
US deliveries over the whole war reached more than 10,000 Javelins, 10,000 TOWs and 3,000 Stingers; the fact sheet gives totals, not arrival dates.
Ukraine kept artillery parity with Russia for about the first six weeks of the invasion, until its ammunition ran short.

The invasion phase featured road-bound Russian columns, weak Russian logistics and C2, and a Ukrainian territorial-defence surge.
UAS attrition in 2022 was extreme: about 90% of drones used were lost.

text: Talks in Belarus and Antalya/Istanbul from 28 February 2022 halted over disagreements and the Bucha massacre.
Mariupol fell to Russia in May 2022.
Russia's Donbas offensive took Sievierodonetsk in June 2022 and then Lysychansk.
Ukraine's Kherson operation began on 29 August 2022, the hinge into the 2022 counteroffensives era.
By summer 2022 Ukraine had used up its own stocks of most critical munitions and depended on partners.
The US delivered 187+ M777 howitzers from April 2022 onward, with Excalibur guided shells.
The US total of 155 mm howitzers delivered to Ukraine eventually passed 200.
The first four HIMARS were in Ukraine by 24 June 2022, and a second four were due by mid-July.
British M270s followed HIMARS into Ukraine from July 2022.
Western precision fires hit Russian logistics in June–July 2022 and took away Russia's advantage of massed artillery supplied from rail-fed depots.
By June 2022 Russia had a 10:1 advantage in volume of fire.
Most Ukrainian losses in 2022 came during the Donbas offensive and the Kherson push, and fell mainly on the professional brigades.
The e2 Donbas phase was a slow, artillery-heavy Russian advance city by city, with very heavy Ukrainian casualties.
The original Russian invasion force proved too small to cover the whole front, which set up Ukraine's autumn 2022 counteroffensives.
Ukraine's Kharkiv counteroffensive began on 6 September 2022.
In the Kharkiv counteroffensive Ukraine retook Balakliia on 8 September, Izium and Kupiansk on 10 September, and Lyman on 1 October 2022.
Ukraine claimed about 12,000 km² and 500+ settlements liberated in the 2022 Kharkiv counteroffensive, while ISW assessed about 2,500 km² for the breakthrough phase alone.
The Russian Western Group of Forces collapsed in the 2022 Kharkiv counteroffensive.
Ukrainian fire control over the Dnipro crossings forced an orderly Russian withdrawal from right-bank Kherson in October–November 2022.
Kherson city was liberated in November 2022.
In autumn 2022 Ukraine had a small pool of ready reserve brigades, with the rest of its force fixed on the line of contact.
The 2022 counteroffensive success spurred the Ramstein pledging process, but agreeing what to gift took about three months, and heavy-armour pledges came only in January 2023.

observations.subject: time to agree what to gift

text: Russia declared partial mobilization on 21 September 2022, with a target of 300,000, followed by a mass exodus of draft-age men.
Russia claimed to annex four partly occupied Ukrainian oblasts on 30 September 2022.
The first Iranian Shahed-136/131 shipment reached Russia in mid-August 2022.
The first Shahed was recovered in Ukraine on 13 September 2022.
The autumn 2022 counteroffensives were the last large Ukrainian manoeuvre successes.
Russia stabilised in late 2022 by trading space (using the Dnipro as a barrier), mobilising, and building fortifications in Zaporizhzhia that would decide the 2023 counteroffensive.
A Russian winter offensive from late January 2023 began at Vuhledar, where Russia lost dozens of armoured vehicles (Reuters via RUSI).
The Russian winter offensive of 2023 spread along the eastern front with its main weight on Bakhmut.
Bakhmut fell to Russia in May 2023.
Western armour was pledged to Ukraine in January 2023.
Leopard 2A4 tanks arrived in Ukraine in February–March 2023 and German Leopard 2A6s in March 2023.
Challenger 2 tanks arrived in Ukraine from March 2023.
Bradley fighting vehicles arrived in Ukraine from April 2023; the US total passed 300.
Ukrainian Patriot crews were trained in early 2023.
The first US and German Patriot batteries arrived in Ukraine in April 2023.
The Ukrainian Air Force put a second Patriot battery on combat duty on 27 April 2023.
Storm Shadow missiles arrived in Ukraine before May 2023.
notes: "before May 2023" — time set to May 2023 as upper bound.

text: Around Bakhmut about 10,000 Ukrainian troops were killed or severely wounded.
From February 2023 Russia had artillery control of Bakhmut's supply roads.
At Bakhmut Russia fought with Wagner plus mobilised convicts, with VDV support.
19,547 Wagner fighters were killed in Bakhmut, 88% of them convicts, and a similar number were seriously wounded.

text: Russia held a 5:1 artillery advantage at Bakhmut.
By March 2023 prisoners were the largest category in Mediazona's count of named Russian dead.
At Bakhmut Russia "traded lives for time" while it built its southern defences.
Ukraine debated whether holding Bakhmut was worth it, fearing that losing it early would expose Chasiv Yar and Kramatorsk.
Lancet loitering munitions emerged as a key Russian precision tool in the Bakhmut era, and by the 2023 counteroffensive were "scouring" the narrow Ukrainian breaches.
Ukrainian supporting attacks at Bakhmut began in mid-May 2023.
The main Orikhiv–Tokmak axis of the 2023 Ukrainian counteroffensive opened on 3 June 2023.
Ukraine used Meteorit line charges to clear lanes through minefields in the 2023 counteroffensive.
The Kakhovka dam was destroyed in the first week of the 2023 counteroffensive.
The Wagner mutiny followed in late June 2023.
A breakthrough in the 2023 counteroffensive was likeliest in early August; by mid-September the goals were tactical.
Krynky, across the Dnipro, was the last attempt of the 2023 Ukrainian offensive.
Over 2023 as a whole the line barely moved: Ukraine lost about 540 km² and regained about 430 km² (DeepState).
The 2023 Ukrainian plan called for 12 armoured and mechanised brigades on a 30 km frontage, isolating Tokmak in 7 days and then reaching Melitopol.
In the event only a couple of Ukrainian brigades were properly equipped for the 2023 offensive, and most were newly raised and undertrained.
At most 55 Ukrainian 155 mm guns fired on the main axis in 2023, at about 70 rounds per gun per day at peak and as low as 10.

The first Abrams tanks arrived in Ukraine on 23 September 2023 (confirmed by Zelensky on 25 September), out of 31 in total, too late for the offensive.
M117 demining vehicles were usable by Ukraine only from October 2023.

text: In 2023 minefields, drones and Lancets, and precision fires made Ukrainian breaching columns predictable and targetable.
Poor Ukrainian operational security meant Russia knew the axis and the timing of the 2023 offensive.
RUSI concluded that renewed Ukrainian offensives would not be viable "in the foreseeable future".
The Battle of Avdiivka opened on 10 October 2023 while the Krynky operation was still under way, so the e6 era overlaps e5 in October–November 2023.
notes: Italic uncited note; cited to the Avdiivka source used in 0043 as background.

text: The e6 era splits at the US supplemental of April 2024; after it Congress made no significant new funding available, but the FY2024 drawdown authority of USD 7.8bn restarted deliveries.
From October 2023 to April 2024 (e6a) Avdiivka fell during the US aid drought, and the Ukrainian shell famine was at its worst.
notes: Uncited sub-phase definition; attached to the block source as background.

text: In May–July 2024 (e6b) the Russian Kharkiv/Vovchansk push was contained and the Russian Pokrovsk drive began.
A third German Patriot battery was pledged in April 2024, and all three German batteries had arrived by July 2024.
The Battle of Avdiivka ran from 10 October 2023 until Syrskyi announced the withdrawal on the evening of 17 February 2024.
The Tavria commander claimed almost 50,000 Russian losses in the Battle of Avdiivka.
After Avdiivka Russia drove west towards Pokrovsk, covering about 50 km from February 2024 to January 2026 at about 70 m/day.
Russia's northern Kharkiv offensive from 10 May 2024 (Vovchansk, Lyptsi) stalled at about 10 km depth.
On 30 May 2024 Washington allowed US weapons to be used against targets in Russia near Kharkiv.

text: Ukrainian troops reported a 5:1 Russian shell advantage in early February 2024, and 8–9:1 at worst, blamed on delayed US and EU packages.
Ukrainian air defence intercepted 77% of Shaheds in February 2024 and 97% in May 2024.
By late 2024 tactical UAVs accounted for 60–70% of damaged or destroyed Russian systems, even though 60–80% of FPVs missed.
The UK MoD counted 30–50 Russian guided munitions a day at Avdiivka by 5 February 2024, or about 600 in four weeks.
About 40,000 UMPK glide-bomb kits were produced in 2024, launched from 30–90 km behind the line.

The OSC counted about 4 million North Korean shells shipped to Russia from September 2023 to April 2025.

text: The e6 era was Russia's firepower-driven attrition against a Ukraine short of ammunition.
Glide bombs "gave the VKS teeth" without air superiority.
The Ukrainian Kursk incursion began on 6 August 2024.
Zelensky claimed 1,250 km² and 92 settlements in Kursk Oblast on 19 August 2024.
Russia's Pokrovsk/Kurakhove drive continued; Russia took Velyka Novosilka by early 2025 and pushed towards the Dnipropetrovsk border.
Russian gains in 2024 totalled about 3,600 km², reaching up to 20 km² a day in November.
Ukraine withdrew from Sudzha on 12 March 2025.
F-16s were confirmed in Ukraine on 4 August 2024, with at least 79 pledged.
Oryx counts about 50 F-16s delivered from the Netherlands, Denmark and Norway, with 53 Belgian jets due from late 2026 to 2030.
The first Dutch F-16s arrived on 6 February 2025.
The first Mirage 2000-5 fighters arrived in Ukraine on 6 February 2025.
Mirage 2000-5s first flew against a Russian strike on 7 March 2025.
France has not given the total of Mirage 2000-5s supplied; Oryx counts 4+ delivered.
Ukraine carried out ATACMS strikes inside Russia from 19 November 2024.
Australia pledged 49 M1A1 Abrams in October 2024, all delivered by December 2025.
In e7 Ukraine had about 800,000 personnel, of which under 25% was usable combat power, holding a 1,200 km line with local force ratios of 1:2 to 1:6.

In early 2025 Russia had about 580,000 troops in its operational group: about 70,000 in Kursk with about 10,000 North Koreans, 80,000 on the Kharkiv axis, 230,000 in Donetsk/Luhansk and about 140,000 in the south.

North Korean troops fought for Russia from November 2024, about 11–12k at first, in company or battalion-sized assaults; Ukrainian troops described them as fit and cohesive.
Russian Shahed/Geran launches rose from about 75 to about 900 a week from September 2024.

text: A Russian thrust towards Dobropillia was halted in August–September 2025.
Over the winter of 2025–26 Ukraine lost most of Pokrovsk and Myrnohrad and withdrew in a "deliberate regrouping".
In 2025 Russia made first inroads into Dnipropetrovsk and Sumy oblasts.
Huliaipole fell to Russia in late December 2025; the Russian 57th Motor Rifle Brigade infiltrated its centre on 17 December against under-manned territorial-defence brigades.
Ukraine retook much of Kupiansk and its surroundings, about 305 km², in late December 2025.
Russian weekly gains peaked again at 141 km² in the last week of January 2026.

Kyiv claims over 40 Russian strategic bombers were destroyed or damaged in Operation Spiderweb.
The SBU's own Spiderweb tally is 41 aircraft hit; independent counts give 12–13 destroyed, and a US estimate says about 20 hit and 10 destroyed.
The US paused aid and intelligence sharing to Ukraine after the 28 February 2025 Oval Office row and lifted the pause on 11 March after Jeddah.
The US Department of Defense paused and resumed deliveries to Ukraine twice in 2025.
New US allocations to Ukraine effectively ended in early 2025; deliveries continued through PURL, created in July 2025.
European military aid to Ukraine in 2025 was 67% above the 2022–24 average, but total military aid was 13% below it.

Russia launched over 50,000 Shaheds in 2025, about 5 times the previous year.
Russian domestic production of the jet Geran-3 began in early 2025.
HUR says Russia recruited 403,000 in 2025, meeting its plan in early December; the 2026 plan is 409,000.
Ukrainian intelligence says North Korea supplied up to 50% of Russia's 122/152 mm ammunition needs by end-2025, plus 148 KN-23/24 missiles by early 2025.

text: Russia used coercive recruitment of migrants and raids in 2025.
By early 2025 the battlefield was transparent within 3 km of the line and watched out to 15 km.
Russian assaults shifted further towards small-group infantry infiltration in 2025; section-size attacks were already the norm in 2024.
Russian 2025 gains were 4,336 km² (DeepState) or 4,831 km² (CSIS), under 1% of Ukraine.
Russia paid about 85 casualties per km² gained in 2025.
At Jeddah in March 2025 a 30-day ceasefire offer was made.
The Trump–Putin Anchorage summit on 15 August 2025 produced no ceasefire.
After Anchorage Trump dropped his ceasefire demand and pressed Kyiv to give up the Donbas "fortress belt" before Zelensky's 18 August 2025 White House visit.
A 28-point US peace plan "very favorable to Russia" (ISW's words) followed in November 2025.
A US–Ukrainian–European 20-point plan followed in December 2025; the Kremlin rejected both it and the 28-point plan as insufficient.
The first Abu Dhabi trilateral round of peace talks was held on 23–24 January 2026.
From late January to May 2026 (e9a) Russia lost Starlink, Ukraine retook 400+ km² on the Oleksandrivka axis by March, Russian net gains dropped to near zero, and there were two holiday truces.
notes: Uncited sub-phase definition; cited as background to the March area-claim source.

text: From June to September 2026 (e9b) came the jet-Geran surge, the Iran-war Patriot shortage, the replacement of the defence minister and commander-in-chief (16–21 July), the 745 km² Oleksandrivka claim (August), Operation Vivaldi made public (September), and envoy diplomacy.
notes: Uncited sub-phase definition. The file places the e9 split at about Jun/Jul 2026 rather than at Vivaldi, which began in late spring.

text: The Starlink cutoff of Russian users was phased, from late January to 5 February 2026.
notes: Summary bullet without its own cite; attached to the MoD sources of the sub-bullets.

text: On 29 January 2026 the Ukrainian MoD contacted SpaceX about Russian use of Starlink.
From late January 2026 a speed cap of about 75–90 km/h hit Starlink-equipped Russian drones.
On 1 February 2026 Musk said SpaceX had taken "effective" steps against Russian use of Starlink at Ukraine's request; this is ISW's "1 Feb" date.
On 2 February 2026 a Ukrainian Cabinet resolution created the Starlink whitelist.
The Starlink whitelist was enforced at about 03:00 Kyiv time on 5 February 2026, when Fedorov said Russian terminals could no longer operate.
Russian Starlink-guided mid-range drone strikes had begun in late December 2025, which probably explains United24's "Dec 2025" date for the cutoff.
General Staff sources said Russia cut, and in places halted, its assaults after the Starlink cutoff.
Russian Telegram throttling followed from 9 February 2026, and ISW judged that it and the Starlink cutoff together degraded Russian C2.
The Starlink cutoff helped the Ukrainian counterattacks of 2026 but did not cause them.
notes: Research-file synthesis heading; cited to the sources of its sub-bullets.

text: The Air Assault Forces (DShV) date their Oleksandrivka-axis offensive from 29 January 2026, the day the MoD first contacted SpaceX and a week before the whitelist was enforced.
Zelensky says the Oleksandrivka offensive was carried out "exactly as it was planned".

ISW first saw "limited and localized" Ukrainian counterattacks on the Dnipropetrovsk–Zaporizhzhia border on 9 February 2026, calling them "opportunistic" and "likely" exploiting the Starlink and Telegram blocks.
A senior NATO official credited the Starlink cutoff for "at least some" of Ukraine's February 2026 gains.

Kostiantyn Mashovets dated the Russian stall from about 8 February 2026, with Ukrainian push-backs of 9–9.5 km along the Yanchur and Haichur rivers; Ukrainian officials still denied it was a "counteroffensive".

The start date of the 2026 southern counterattacks ranges from 29 January (DShV's own dating) to 9 February (the first open-source observation); an 11 February date came only from Wikipedia and is dropped.
notes: Research-file synthesis; uncited line.

text: How much ground Ukraine retook in 2026 depends on who is counting and on whether grey-zone clearing counts as "liberation"; Syrskyi preferred "restored control".
Zelensky claimed 300 km² retaken on the Oleksandrivka axis on 20 February 2026.
Zelensky claimed 435 km² on 8 March 2026, and Syrskyi claimed 285.6 km² for one Air Assault grouping alone on 9 March.
Syrskyi called February–March 2026 the first month since Kursk 2024 in which Ukraine regained more territory than it lost.
notes: The text says "the first month since Kursk 2024"; the exact month is not stated beyond the March 2026 report.

text: The DShV claimed 745 km² and 26 settlements retaken by 12 August 2026 (12 in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, 10 in Donetsk and 4 in Zaporizhzhia), plus 300+ km² of rear areas cleared of infiltrators.

text: Zelensky claims 9,550 Russians were killed in the January–August 2026 Oleksandrivka operation.
Smaller Ukrainian pushes, such as 46 km² near Novoselivka (29 May 2026, DeepState), continued through the spring.
The Kyiv Independent cautioned that most 2026 Ukrainian advances visible in open sources were extended clearing operations in a wide grey zone rather than breaches of Russian defence lines.
ISW later called the Oleksandrivka effort a counteroffensive.

Operation Vivaldi near Lyman was run by the 3rd Army Corps under Biletskyi, whose units include the 60th Mechanised Brigade, the 125th Heavy Mechanised Brigade and a battalion tactical group of the 3rd Assault Brigade.

text: Russian and OSINT sources tracked the Vivaldi attacks from late spring 2026, and the 3rd Army Corps revealed the operation only on 15 September.
In Vivaldi phase 1, announced 15 September 2026, the 3rd Army Corps claimed 75 km² cleared of infiltrators plus 10 km² liberated (Novoselivka, Oleksandrivka, Yarova and Serednie).

text: The second Abu Dhabi round on 4–5 February 2026 produced a 314-person exchange and no ceasefire; a short energy-strike moratorium was in force at the time.

text: During the 2026 Easter truce long-range strikes paused for about a day, but artillery, FPVs and assaults did not.
Ukraine declared a unilateral Victory Day ceasefire from 6 May 2026, which Russia ignored.
Ukraine and Russia then agreed a 9–11 May 2026 ceasefire with a POW exchange; the Kremlin restated that Ukraine must withdraw from the rest of Donetsk Oblast before any ceasefire.
During the 9–11 May 2026 ceasefire limited fighting went on, and Russia used the pause to rotate and resupply.
During the US envoys' visit, Kyiv and Moscow halted long-range strikes on each other's capitals from 5 to 7 September 2026.
Ukrainian brigades were ordered to hold fire along the front from 5 to 8 September 2026, a truce Ukraine proposed and Putin rejected.
On 6 September 2026 Zelensky and Witkoff/Kushner agreed "fundamental principles", including security and economic guarantees, while Putin restated maximalist aims.
CSMonitor reports that Zelensky rejected the terms of the September 2026 US plan, contrary to other accounts.
On 14 September 2026 Trump announced a mutual "energy ceasefire"; Zelensky offered one on condition of reciprocity, and Russia did not respond.
By 25 September 2026 Putin was signalling a winter strike campaign instead of an energy ceasefire.

In 2026, for the first time since 2022, Ukraine regained the local initiative, through drone-led, information-silent operations against infiltrators and their supply lines rather than mechanised breakthroughs.
In 2026 the strategic air war escalated in quality (jet Gerans, ballistic missiles against a Patriot shortage) as much as in quantity.
